scenes.heading: Introduction to surds
scenes.say: A square has an area of two square centimetres. How long is each side? No fraction works exactly. The answer is root two, and numbers like it are called surds.
scenes.caption: A square has an area of 2 cm². How long is each side? No fraction works exactly. The answer is √2, and numbers like it are called surds.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: 9 tiles make a 3 by 3 square, but 10 tiles never make a square
scenes.science: √9 = 3 exactly, but √10 is a surd between 3 and 4
scenes.breaks: Tiles come in whole pieces, but a real square can have any area, like 10.5 cm².
scenes.say: Think of square tiles. Nine tiles make a perfect three by three square, so root nine is three. Try ten tiles and there is always a gap. The side would be somewhere between three and four, and you can never write it exactly as a fraction. That is a surd: root ten.
scenes.caption: Nine tiles make a perfect 3 by 3 square, so √9 = 3. Try ten tiles and there is always a gap. The side is between 3 and 4, and you can never write it exactly as a fraction. That is a surd: √10.

scenes.heading: A square with area 2
scenes.say: First the square, then its area: two square centimetres. Each side must multiply by itself to give two, so the side is root two centimetres. Its decimal is one point four one four two, and it goes on forever without repeating.
scenes.caption: Here is the square, with area 2 cm². Each side must multiply by itself to give 2, so the side is √2 cm. Its decimal is 1.4142… and it goes on forever without repeating.

scenes.heading: Surds live on the number line
scenes.say: Every surd has a place on the number line. First the line, then the dots for root two, root three and root five. To place root five, sandwich five between the perfect squares four and nine. So root five is between two and three, closer to two.
scenes.caption: Every surd has a place on the number line: here are √2, √3 and √5. To place √5, sandwich 5 between the perfect squares 4 and 9. So √5 is between 2 and 3, closer to 2.

scenes.heading: Surd rules
scenes.say: Root a times root b equals root of a b. Dividing works the same way. Root a, squared, is just a. But adding does not work: root nine plus root sixteen is three plus four, seven, not root twenty-five.
scenes.caption: √a × √b = √(ab). Dividing works the same way. (√a)² = a. But adding does not work: √9 + √16 = 3 + 4 = 7, not √25.

scenes.heading: Exact length
scenes.question: A right-angled triangle has shorter sides 2 cm and 3 cm. Find the exact hypotenuse.
scenes.say: A right-angled triangle has shorter sides two and three centimetres. Pythagoras: c squared equals two squared plus three squared, which is four plus nine, thirteen. Thirteen is not a perfect square, so the exact answer is root thirteen centimetres.
scenes.caption: Shorter sides 2 cm and 3 cm. Pythagoras: c² = 2² + 3² = 4 + 9 = 13. 13 is not a perfect square, so the exact answer is √13 cm.

points: Surd: a root that never ends or repeats
scenes.say: Recap. A surd is a root whose decimal never ends or repeats. Roots of perfect squares are not surds. Estimate by sandwiching between perfect squares. Multiply and divide under one root, square to undo a root, and never add under the root. Now try the practice questions!
